### Support Vector Machine (SVM)

An SVM finds the boundary that separates the two classes with the widest margin.
A **linear kernel** fits a straight boundary, much like logistic regression. A
**radial (RBF) kernel** can fit curved boundaries. We tune both with 10-fold
cross-validation on the training set only. `cost` controls how heavily
misclassified training points are penalized, and `gamma` controls how flexible
the radial boundary is. Predictors are standardized automatically
(`scale = TRUE`), which matters because SVMs are distance-based.

```{r svm-tune-linear}
set.seed(380)
tune_linear <- tune(svm, HeartDisease ~ ., data = train, kernel = "linear",
                    ranges = list(cost = c(0.01, 0.1, 1, 10)),
                    tunecontrol = tune.control(cross = 10))
summary(tune_linear)
```

```{r svm-tune-radial}
set.seed(380)
tune_radial <- tune(svm, HeartDisease ~ ., data = train, kernel = "radial",
                    ranges = list(cost  = c(0.1, 1, 10, 100),
                                  gamma = c(0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.5)),
                    tunecontrol = tune.control(cross = 10))
tune_radial$best.parameters
tune_radial$best.performance   # CV error rate
```

```{r svm-tune-plot, fig.height=3.5}
ggplot(tune_radial$performances,
       aes(factor(gamma), factor(cost), fill = error)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(error, 3)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "firebrick") +
  labs(title = "Radial SVM: 10-fold CV error by cost and gamma",
       x = "gamma", y = "cost", fill = "CV error") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r svm-cv-compare}
data.frame(
  kernel   = c("linear", "radial"),
  best     = c(paste("cost =", tune_linear$best.parameters$cost),
               paste("cost =", tune_radial$best.parameters$cost,
                     ", gamma =", tune_radial$best.parameters$gamma)),
  CV_error = round(c(tune_linear$best.performance,
                     tune_radial$best.performance), 3)
)
```

Next we refit both tuned models on the full training set with
`probability = TRUE`, so they also output probabilities for the ROC curve.

```{r svm-final}
svm_linear <- svm(HeartDisease ~ ., data = train, kernel = "linear",
                  cost = tune_linear$best.parameters$cost, probability = TRUE)
svm_radial <- svm(HeartDisease ~ ., data = train, kernel = "radial",
                  cost  = tune_radial$best.parameters$cost,
                  gamma = tune_radial$best.parameters$gamma,
                  probability = TRUE)

svm_eval <- function(model, name) {
  pred <- predict(model, test, probability = TRUE)
  prob <- attr(pred, "probabilities")[, "1"]
  cm   <- confusionMatrix(pred, test$HeartDisease, positive = "1")
  list(name = name, pred = pred, prob = prob, cm = cm,
       roc = roc(test$HeartDisease, prob, levels = c("0", "1"),
                 direction = "<", quiet = TRUE))
}
res_linear <- svm_eval(svm_linear, "SVM (linear)")
res_radial <- svm_eval(svm_radial, "SVM (radial)")

res_radial$cm$table   # confusion matrix: rows = predicted, columns = actual
```

```{r svm-results}
get_metrics <- function(r) {
  data.frame(Model       = r$name,
             Accuracy    = round(r$cm$overall["Accuracy"], 3),
             Sensitivity = round(r$cm$byClass["Sensitivity"], 3),
             Specificity = round(r$cm$byClass["Specificity"], 3),
             AUC         = round(as.numeric(auc(r$roc)), 3))
}
baseline <- data.frame(Model = "Baseline (always 'disease')",
                       Accuracy = round(mean(test$HeartDisease == "1"), 3),
                       Sensitivity = 1, Specificity = 0, AUC = 0.5)
svm_results <- rbind(baseline, get_metrics(res_linear), get_metrics(res_radial))
rownames(svm_results) <- NULL
svm_results
```

```{r svm-roc, fig.height=4, fig.width=5}
roc_list <- setNames(list(res_radial$roc, res_linear$roc),
                     c(sprintf("Radial (AUC = %.3f)", auc(res_radial$roc)),
                       sprintf("Linear (AUC = %.3f)", auc(res_linear$roc))))
ggroc(roc_list, legacy.axes = TRUE, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey") +
  labs(title = "SVM ROC curves (test set)", x = "1 - Specificity",
       y = "Sensitivity", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = c(0.7, 0.2))
```

```{r svm-export}
# Save for the "Comparing Results" section
svm_test_probs <- data.frame(actual = test$HeartDisease,
                             svm_linear = res_linear$prob,
                             svm_radial = res_radial$prob)
```

**SVM interpretation:** both SVMs clearly beat the baseline, with 88.6% test
accuracy versus 55.4%. Sensitivity is 0.89, so they catch about 9 of every 10
heart disease cases; specificity is 0.88 and AUC is 0.93. In cross-validation
the linear kernel did slightly better than the radial one (12.9% vs. 13.2%
error), and on the test set the two give identical results. Tuning also picked
the smallest gamma (0.001) for the radial kernel, which makes its boundary
nearly straight. In other words, the flexible kernel gains nothing here,
which suggests the relationship between the predictors and heart disease is
close to linear. That supports using the more interpretable logistic
regression. Unlike
logistic regression, an SVM gives no coefficients or odds ratios, so it tells
us how well heart disease *can* be predicted but not *which* variables drive
the prediction.
